title: Bill's Turtle Trading Journey, Modern Systematic Trading, and more!  - Open Interest 10

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Bill's Turtle Trading Journey, Modern Systematic Trading, and more!  - Open Interest 10.docx

speakers: Bill Eckhardt (guest, co-creator of the Turtle system, Eckhardt Trading Company)
Rob Santino (guest, president and COO, Eckhardt Trading Company)
summary:
Eckhardt and Santino discuss the Turtle origins and how ETC evolved from published breakout rules: risk control first (utility theory), avoiding overfitting and underfitting, the E-score and Gauntlet testing process.
Key views: futures returns are heavy-tailed so use robust statistics and long samples; reject high win-rate strategies; keep position sizes constant, no vol targeting; diversify to ~70 liquid markets; avoid stocks and CTA replication.

ballistics analogy, ETC as research lab, risk aversion and prediction futility

completeness_estimate: 0.90 - first reader caught the core risk-control, fitting and statistics claims; missed several host elaborations (hidden mean reversion, SD vs normality, Mandelbrot evidence, long-term robustness) and Santino's replication call; one speaker error.

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: the structure of the market is that the money flows from the many to the few so you have to be among the few not among the many
claims.claim: Money flows from the many to the few, so normal human reflexes put you among the many and losing; successful trading feels unpleasant and requires suffering and not following inclinations.

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: there's more to trading than Simply Having rules you have risk management
claims.claim: Trading success needs more than entry rules: risk management and attitudes toward profit and loss; Dennis ran the Turtles' risk control while Eckhardt developed rules.

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: it was much harder to mechanize what is needed for trading
claims.claim: Eckhardt thought mechanizing trading (versus Dennis' 'weighted rules' view) was much harder than it seemed.

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: I have formalized certain parts of trading in a mathematically rigorous fashion
claims.claim: His approach was to build a theory of trading from the philosophy of science, formalizing pieces rigorously rather than a complete theory.

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: because you have to oversimplify a problem sometimes in the beginning
claims.claim: Like ballistics, a trading theory starts oversimplified (few factors) and improves as research adds relevant factors.

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: we can't be very successful about predicting where the Market's going to go it's too close
claims.claim: Markets are not random but too close to random for simple predictions, so focus should be on risk control, which one can know and control, rather than prediction.
claims.direction: focus on risk control not prediction

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: instead you have to focus on risk control because that's something you you can know your risk you can change your risk you can control your risk
claims.claim: Do not predict the market; decide what to do wherever it goes: risk control first, with profitability following from correct risk control.

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: every dollar every new dollar that you make is a little smaller than the last one and more importantly every dollar that you lose is the little bigger than the last
claims.claim: Utility theory: marginal utility of money diminishes, so losses weigh more than gains and risk aversion is a rigorous concept; ETC uses a small class of utility functions suited to commodity trading and client circumstances.
claims.testable: partly - utility-based sizing can be tested

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: they graft risk control almost as an afterthought on their system on their profitability system
claims.claim: Most traders build a profitable system first and graft risk control on afterwards; ETC brings expected utility in at the ground floor of research and judges every idea by its effect on expected utility.

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: the risk loving ones to be died these are utility functions for somebody who wants to keep betting the ranch and eventually I think they're financially suicidal
claims.claim: Risk-neutral and risk-loving utility functions lead to ruin (the St Petersburg paradox shows absurd infinite expected value bets).

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: one has to be risk averse that's the only thing that can that can work in this business
claims.claim: In futures trading with leverage, risk aversion is primary since risk-loving traders repeatedly lose all their money.

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: we have shortterm we have medium we have long-term systems but you know we have trades that that have a a four or five day average length
claims.claim: ETC runs short, medium and long-term systems with average trade lengths from 4-5 days to 50-60 days.

claims.speaker: Moritz Seibert
claims.quote: they have moved over to longer term hold periods because of the Alpha DK that we could deserve observe in the shorter term systems
claims.claim: Many Turtle students moved to longer holding periods because of alpha decay in short-term systems.
claims.testable: partly - trend returns by horizon over time

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: they've been heavily degraded since we let the turtles go and all all this information got revealed
claims.claim: Turtle rules (breakout systems) were widely published so their edge was degraded by competition; Eckhardt moved to different trend-following systems even before they were released.

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: the death of trend following has been highly exaggerated
claims.claim: Trend following has been declared dead every few years; the majority of ETC's work is still trend following with a small non-trend part.
claims.testable: yes - long history of trend returns

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: one has to keep researching to stay ahead of it
claims.claim: Red Queen effect: with more competition and technical analysis knowledge, a commodity trader must improve as fast as possible just to hold his own.

claims.speaker: Rob Santino
claims.quote: volatility enters into our trading system in several different ways and about five or six different ways
claims.claim: Volatility enters ETC's systems in five or six ways (position sizing, measuring price change, risk control) alongside price, so the systems are based on both.

claims.speaker: Rob Santino
claims.quote: in a lot of situations um increased volatility often helps us we don't want to restrain it
claims.claim: ETC does not target portfolio volatility because higher volatility often helps trend systems and they do not want to juice up when volatility is low; they track individual futures' volatility for risk.

claims.speaker: Rob Santino
claims.quote: since um volatility often increases with a trend we have found that and if we were readjusting to volatility we would
claims.claim: Position sizes are kept roughly constant from entry to exit: readjusting to rising volatility would cut the position along with the trend, which they found counterproductive.
claims.testable: yes - test dynamic vs constant size

claims.speaker: Moritz Seibert
claims.quote: which means controlled risk and therefore a sythetic long optionality profile if you will
claims.claim: Constant sizing with a stop-loss gives controlled risk and a synthetic long-optionality (volatility-seeking) profile.

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: it's volatility that mean reverts uh price doesn't doesn't mean revert at least Futures prices
claims.claim: ETC's non-trend methods (about 20% of work) are not mean reversion because futures prices do not mean revert while volatility does.

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: instead of boiling all the structure down into one number you're keeping some of the structure
claims.claim: Summary statistics of signals (e.g. a moving average) throw away structure; keeping the 20-day high and low gives more information (position within the range).

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: what you have to do is you have to find out you have to eliminate a lot of the structure but you have to keep enough of it
claims.claim: Keeping all price-history structure is combinatorially impossible, so research must eliminate structure but keep what is important.

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: it's appropriate to estimate volatility using moving averages
claims.claim: Volatility is a moving-average process, so moving averages suit volatility, but price is non-stationary and not an MA process, so moving averages and crossovers on price are counterproductive.
claims.indicator: moving average on price vs volatility

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: to try to fit to the permanent features of the time series whereas you want to ignore the transitory features
claims.claim: Fitting should capture permanent features and ignore transitory ones; some overfitting is inevitable, so ETC uses in-house techniques to estimate and minimize overfit.

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: if you're afraid of overfitting one way is to underfit
claims.claim: Underfitting is also bad because it ignores worthwhile market information; some good traders lost all their money from overfitting.

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: a system might make too much of its money over too short a period of time well we have elements of the escore which which will test for that
claims.claim: The E-score combines many performance measures (a 'Super Value') and discounts systems that earned most profit in a short span (e.g. 2 of 20 years), guarding against false impressions of quality.

claims.speaker: Rob Santino
claims.quote: bill has spent as much time uh tearing systems apart as we do putting them together
claims.claim: The Gauntlet is a barrage of tests designed to tear a system apart, showing where it fails, which is as important as knowing why it works, and removes emotion.

claims.speaker: Rob Santino
claims.quote: you could have systems that they might have a two three four month really strong run and then they just go flat or degrade
claims.claim: Systems can have a strong 2-4 month run then go flat, so scientific testing and emotion removal are needed.

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: it actually tests the program too it can find very subtle glitches in the program
claims.claim: The Gauntlet also tests the program code and finds subtle glitches that would otherwise be nearly impossible to find.

claims.speaker: Moritz Seibert
claims.quote: the more markets we trade the more independent bets we can place um the better we can crystallize our Edge over time
claims.claim: More markets give more independent bets and less noise in any run, though smaller portfolios can outperform for periods because of concentration.
claims.testable: yes - performance vs number of markets

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: we measure the liquidity and the trade slippage for all markets that we trade whether we're considering trading
claims.claim: ETC trades about 70 markets, believes in diversification as the greatest financial idea of the 20th century, but avoids markets with too much slippage or too little liquidity.

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: on paper these Alternatives markets might appear better but in practice I I think they're actually worse
claims.claim: Alternative markets look better in backtests but slippage and exit difficulty in a hurry make them worse in practice.

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: stocks don't really have the kind of robust Trend component that Futures tend to have in other words our systems don't apply very well to stocks
claims.claim: Single stocks have a weaker trend component than futures (splits, dividends, long-dominated), so ETC specialises in futures where it has relative advantage.
claims.indicator: trend strength in stocks vs futures
claims.testable: yes - compare trend returns by asset

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: whereas in the Futures Market there is exactly one long for every short and vice versa it's completely balanced
claims.claim: Futures are balanced (one long per short) while stock markets are dominated by longs, so they are different processes.

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: here's a fundamental fact and that is that the distribution the probability distribution of price change and also of trades in a Futures Trading System are not normally distributed
claims.claim: Replicating CTA indices by regression 'sounds like an invitation to really overfit'; futures price changes and trade results are radically non-normal.

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: you need to avoid normal techniques and you need to use what statisticians call robust or distribution free statistics
claims.claim: Use robust, distribution-free statistics because futures returns are heavy tailed (Mandelbrot: possibly no variance); small-sample normal statistics give wrong answers, standard deviation and least-squares correlation are unreliable.
claims.testable: yes - compare robust vs normal estimates

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: the drawback of such robust statistics is that they're kind of data Hogs you need 10 20 time 30 times as much data to make a reliable inference
claims.claim: Robust statistics need 10-30 times more data, so ETC needs 10-20 years of data and cannot conclude anything from two or three years (that is overfitting).

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: busted out spectacularly and it really was because they were using normal distribution Theory
claims.claim: LTCM failed because it relied on normal distribution theory despite fat tails.

claims.speaker: Rob Santino
claims.quote: keeping these losses small is what keeps you in business
claims.claim: Replication portfolios lack predefined exits, exposing them to discontinuity and gap events; stops and exit rules keeping losses small are essential.

correction.issue: Wrong speaker: the point that replication portfolios lack predefined exits and that keeping losses small keeps you in business is made by host Moritz Seibert (he opens 'and Rob maybe to your point'); Eckhardt then agrees.
correction.fix: Moritz Seibert: regression-based replication portfolios lack predefined exits, exposing them to discontinuity and gap events; stops and exit rules that keep losses small are essential.

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: the left hand tail the one that represents losses is very heavy
claims.claim: All futures markets have heavy left tails (leptokurtosis), so trading rules must intervene to control the left tail via risk management.

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: they make money 70 80 90% of the time but then they're subject to large freakish losses
claims.claim: High win-rate strategies (selling cheap options) periodically bust out because they exploit the bulk of the distribution; ETC rejects any new system with 70-80% success and prefers a ~40% success rate with larger winners.
claims.testable: yes - win rate vs tail loss

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: you almost never know better than about 51 or 52% which way the Market's going
claims.claim: Predictive accuracy is about 51-52%, so put ten times as much emphasis on risk control as on prediction.

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: you have to get out of your losses you have to let your profits run
claims.claim: Normal human attitudes (hold losers) are dead wrong; traders must cut losses and let profits run.

claims.speaker: Moritz Seibert
claims.quote: this pain Arbitrage of sticking to your system during bad times when the going gets tough and nobody enjoys it
claims.claim: The trend follower's edge is a pain arbitrage: enduring bad periods while keeping individual losses small.

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: there were some who dropped out you know fairly soon and that that indicated that they didn't have the right emotional makeup
claims.claim: Some Turtle trainees dropped out or could not get along, which showed they lacked the right emotional makeup.

claims.speaker: Moritz Seibert
claims.quote: the longer term systems you know two and a day time frames things like that to the present day they continue to work and they go up and down and they're robust
claims.claim: While short-term trend systems show alpha decay, longer-term trend systems (around 200-day look-backs) still work and remain robust, with drawdowns.
claims.testable: yes - compare short vs long look-back trend returns over time

claims.speaker: Moritz Seibert
claims.quote: essentially executing a hidden Mar reversion trade against the direction of the trend that is not always true by definition but uh it is true in my experience more often than not
claims.claim: Resizing an open trend position to rising volatility amounts to a hidden mean-reversion trade against the trend, because volatility usually rises as the trend extends.
claims.direction: do not cut trend positions as volatility rises
claims.conditions: when volatility rises with the trend (usual but not always)
claims.testable: yes - backtest constant vs vol-resized position sizing

claims.speaker: Bill Eckhardt
claims.quote: I still think a lot of Traders just like to jump on the latest bandwagon you know the latest few things that are hot and avoid everything else you know they're they're anti- diversifying
claims.claim: Many traders undercut diversification by concentrating on whichever few markets are currently hot, which is anti-diversification despite its proven value.
claims.testable: partly - compare concentrated hot-market portfolios vs broad ones

claims.speaker: Rob Santino
claims.quote: I think on the replication question that's probably not going to have a good ending
claims.claim: Regression-based CTA-index replication products are likely to end badly.
claims.testable: yes - replication ETF performance vs CTA indices over time

claims.speaker: Moritz Seibert
claims.quote: it is definitely tailed in both directions it is prone to jumps
claims.claim: Evidence cited from Mandelbrot's cotton-price work: futures returns are fat-tailed on both sides and jump-prone, possibly a stable Paretian distribution without a defined variance.
claims.testable: yes - tail-index estimation on futures returns

claims.speaker: Moritz Seibert
claims.quote: many people would calculate volatility as a function of standard deviation under the assumption of normal distribution there you go again you're back
claims.claim: Computing volatility as a standard deviation for sizing reintroduces normal-distribution assumptions and their drawbacks; range-based measures like ATR are not standard deviations.
claims.testable: yes - compare sizing with SD vs ATR/robust estimators
